Eleventh Indian Expedition to Antarctica, Scientific Report, 1995 
Department ofOcean Development, Technical Publication No. 9, pp. 53-78 
Report on the Meteorological Programme Carried Out 
During Eleventh Indian Expedition to Antarctica 
A.L. KOPPAR 
India Meteorological Department 
Shivaji Nagar,Pune - 411 005 
Abstract 
India Meteorological Department has an on-going meteorological programme in the 
Antarctic Expeditions. During the eleventh expedition, two new sub programmes viz.,Slow 
rising Low Level Radiosonde and Pilot Balloon ascents were added on experimental basis. 
In this report data pertaining to surface weather, vertical distribution of ozone and global 
solar radiation have been presented and discussed. Data on radiometersonde and low level 
radiosonde ascents and sunphotorneter observations could not be included as these are still 
being processed. Pilot Balloon ascents were not successful due to early bursting of balloon 
and difficulty in tracking in cold environment. 
Introduction 
The meteorological programme of India Meteorological Department, in 
Antarctica, is of on-going nature. During the eleventh expedition, however, two 
new sub-programmes were included. These are Low Level Slow Rising Ra-
diosonde ascents (LLSR-RS) for  determining the temperature and  humidity 
profiles in the lowest few kilometres of the atmosphere and Pilot Balloon (PB) 
ascents for determining the upper level winds. Both the programmes had been 
included on an experimental basis. 
The on-going  observational  programmes  included  continuous  surface 
weather watch,  weekly  measurement  of  vertical distribution  of  ozone, and 
fortnightly measurement of infra-red radiation fluxes in the upper atmosphere. 
During onward and return cruise of the expedition from India to Antarctica and 
back, daily recording of surface and upper air observations formed part of the 
programme. 
54 
Results and Discussions 
Presented here are the data pertaining to surface weather, vertical distribu-
tion of ozone and global solar radiation. Data on radiometersonde, low level 
radiosonde ascents  are  still  under  process. Pilot  balloon  ascents  were  not 
successful due to early bursting of balloons. Also, tracking of balloon was very 
difficult due to extreme cold. 
Data of surface weather originates from 3 hourly manual synoptic obser-
vations and continuous recording of some parameters like pressure, temperature 
and wind  by  autographic  instruments.  Weather  charts  and  satellite  cloud 
Imageries were also received on most of the days. 
The climatic data  of 1992  are presented in  Table I and  mean  monthly 
variation in  pressure, temperature and  wind are  shown in  Fig 1.  Individual 
meteorological elements are discussed below. 
a) Mean sea-level pressure 
Mean sea-level pressure varied between 978.7 hPa and 994.9 hPa. Seasonal 
variation in pressure was not very clear but the trend of alternately rising and 
failing with humps in summer and winter and sinks in autumn and spring, is 
discernible. There seems to be some time lag between the seasons and pressure 
response. During 1992 the lowest pressure of 952.2 hPa was recorded on April 
16 and highest pressure of 1015.9 hPa was recorded on June 27. 
b) Air temperature 
Mean monthly air  temperature shows  systematic  variation  with highest 
mean value of +1.3 °C in January and lowest mean value of -18.9°C in August. 
It decreased continuously from January to August and increased rapidly there-
after. 
Average maximum  and  minimum  temperatures  also  show  similar 
trend.Highest maximum temperature of+7.8°C was recorded on January 2 and 
lowest minimum temperature of -31.7°C was recorded on August 29. 
Day today temperature variation at Maitri is governed by two factors viz., 
(i) day and  night cycle and (ii) warm air advection from northern latitudes in 
the wake  of depressions. In  exclusion of the second factor, diurnal  variation 
(Fig 2) is small but rhythmic in equinoxial months (4-5°C). Minimum tempera-
ture is attained by about 0600 UTC (0640 LAT) and maximum is attained by 
1200 UTC. During summer solstice the diurnal variation is comparatively more 
pronounced (7 °C). In  peak summer month when the Sun shines continuously,
